### Problem: All Assign Point Add {#sec-ds-p5-assign}

::: {.p-statement}
You are given an array $A_1, \ldots, A_N$ and $Q$ queries, processed in order:

- `1 x` — assign $x$ to **every** element of $A$;
- `2 i x` — add $x$ to $A_i$;
- `3 i` — print $A_i$.

$1 \le N, Q \le 2\cdot10^5$, $0 \le A_i, x \le 10^9$, and at least one query is of type 3. Values can exceed $2^{31}$ (sample 2 adds $10^9$ seven times to $10^9$ and prints $8\cdot10^9$). Sample 1: $A = (3, 1, 4, 1, 5)$ with queries `3 2`, `2 3 4`, `3 3`, `1 1`, `2 3 4`, `3 3` prints `1, 8, 5`.

Source: [AC abc278_d · All Assign Point Add](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc278/tasks/abc278_d){.solved}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
An "assign everything" query is a reset to a value, and doing it cell by cell is $O(N)$, so $Q$ of them cost $O(NQ)$. Do it lazily instead (@sec-ds-a5): remember the assigned value and a clock that counts assignments. Each cell keeps the clock reading at its last write; a cell whose stamp is older than the clock is logically equal to the last assigned value, and is brought up to date only when a query touches it.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Eager.** Type 1 writes all $N$ cells. $O(N)$ per assignment, $O(NQ)$ total, too slow at $2\cdot10^5 \times 2\cdot10^5$. This function is the model for the stress test.
2. **Reset only the touched cells.** After an assignment, only the cells changed by later type 2 queries differ from the base value. Keep `base` and a list of touched indices; an assignment resets only those cells (to "no offset") and sets `base`. Each touched index is reset once per time it was touched, so the total is $O(N + Q)$.
3. **Timestamps.** Keep `base`, a clock `epoch` (number of assignments so far) and `stamp[i]`. Before reading or adding at $i$, *refresh* it: if `stamp[i] != epoch`, set `val[i] = base`, `stamp[i] = epoch`. An assignment is `base = x; epoch += 1`. Every query is $O(1)$ worst case.

**Operation contract (final form).** Invariant **I**: the true value of $A_i$ is `val[i]` if `stamp[i] == epoch`, and `base` otherwise.

| Query | What it does | How **I** survives | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1 x` | `base = x`; `epoch += 1` | every stamp is now older than `epoch`, so every cell reads `base = x`, which is the truth | $O(1)$ |
| `2 i x` | refresh $i$, then `val[i] += x` | after the refresh `stamp[i] == epoch`, so `val[i]` is the true value before and after the add | $O(1)$ |
| `3 i` | refresh $i$, print `val[i]` | refresh does not change the true value | $O(1)$ |
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Eager

::: {.form-next}
Exactly what the statement says. Correct, and $O(N)$ per assignment.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def assign_add_eager(a, queries):
    a = list(a)
    out = []
    for q in queries:
        if q[0] == 1:
            for i in range(len(a)):
                a[i] = q[1]
        elif q[0] == 2:
            a[q[1] - 1] += q[2]
        else:
            out.append(a[q[1] - 1])
    return out


AA_S1 = ([3, 1, 4, 1, 5], [(3, 2), (2, 3, 4), (3, 3), (1, 1), (2, 3, 4), (3, 3)], [1, 8, 5])
AA_S2 = ([10 ** 9], [(2, 1, 10 ** 9)] * 7 + [(3, 1)], [8 * 10 ** 9])
AA_S3 = ([1, 8, 4, 15, 7, 5, 7, 5, 8, 0],
         [(2, 7, 0), (3, 7), (3, 8), (1, 7), (3, 3), (2, 4, 4), (2, 4, 9), (2, 10, 5), (1, 10),
          (2, 4, 2), (1, 10), (2, 3, 1), (2, 8, 11), (2, 3, 14), (2, 1, 9), (3, 8), (3, 8),
          (3, 1), (2, 6, 5), (3, 7)],
         [7, 5, 7, 21, 21, 19, 10])
for a, qs, want in (AA_S1, AA_S2, AA_S3):
    assert assign_add_eager(a, qs) == want
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<long long> assignAddEager(vector<long long> a, const vector<vector<long long>>& qs) {
    vector<long long> out;
    for (const auto& q : qs) {
        if (q[0] == 1) fill(a.begin(), a.end(), q[1]);
        else if (q[0] == 2) a[q[1] - 1] += q[2];
        else out.push_back(a[q[1] - 1]);
    }
    return out;
}
```
:::

#### Reset only the touched cells

::: {.form-next}
Split each value into `base + off[i]`. An assignment must zero every `off[i]`, but only the cells in the `touched` list can be non-zero, so it resets those and empties the list. A cell enters the list once per add, so the resets cost $O(Q)$ in total. This is the **dirty list** form of a lazy reset.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def assign_add_dirty(a, queries):
    base, off = 0, list(a)               # value of cell i is base + off[i]
    touched = list(range(len(a)))        # every off[i] may be non-zero at the start
    out = []
    for q in queries:
        if q[0] == 1:
            for i in touched:
                off[i] = 0
            touched.clear()
            base = q[1]
        elif q[0] == 2:
            off[q[1] - 1] += q[2]
            touched.append(q[1] - 1)
        else:
            out.append(base + off[q[1] - 1])
    return out


for a, qs, want in (AA_S1, AA_S2, AA_S3):
    assert assign_add_dirty(a, qs) == want
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<long long> assignAddDirty(const vector<long long>& a, const vector<vector<long long>>& qs) {
    long long base = 0;
    vector<long long> off(a);
    vector<int> touched;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) touched.push_back(i);
    vector<long long> out;
    for (const auto& q : qs) {
        if (q[0] == 1) { for (int i : touched) off[i] = 0; touched.clear(); base = q[1]; }
        else if (q[0] == 2) { off[q[1] - 1] += q[2]; touched.push_back((int)q[1] - 1); }
        else out.push_back(base + off[q[1] - 1]);
    }
    return out;
}
```
:::

#### Timestamps

::: {.form-next}
No list at all: an assignment only bumps the clock, and each cell refreshes itself when a query touches it. Every query is $O(1)$ worst case, which the dirty list only achieves amortised (one assignment may reset many cells at once). The stress test compares both lazy forms with the eager model on random arrays and query lists.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def assign_add(a, queries):
    val = list(a)
    stamp = [0] * len(a)
    epoch, base = 0, 0                   # the initial values are "written at epoch 0"
    out = []

    def refresh(i):
        if stamp[i] != epoch:            # stale: the true value is the last assigned base
            val[i] = base
            stamp[i] = epoch

    for q in queries:
        if q[0] == 1:
            base, epoch = q[1], epoch + 1
        elif q[0] == 2:
            refresh(q[1] - 1)
            val[q[1] - 1] += q[2]
        else:
            refresh(q[1] - 1)
            out.append(val[q[1] - 1])
    return out


for a, qs, want in (AA_S1, AA_S2, AA_S3):
    assert assign_add(a, qs) == want      # AA_S1 is the board sample: 1, 8, 5
# stress: random arrays and queries against the eager model
for _ in range(400):
    n = random.randint(1, 6)
    a = [random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(n)]
    qs = []
    for _ in range(random.randint(1, 25)):
        t = random.randint(1, 3)
        qs.append((1, random.randint(0, 9)) if t == 1 else
                  (2, random.randint(1, n), random.randint(0, 9)) if t == 2 else
                  (3, random.randint(1, n)))
    want = assign_add_eager(a, qs)
    assert assign_add(a, qs) == want == assign_add_dirty(a, qs)
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int n, q;
    scanf("%d", &n);
    vector<long long> val(n);
    for (auto& v : val) scanf("%lld", &v);
    vector<int> stamp(n, 0);
    int epoch = 0;
    long long base = 0;
    scanf("%d", &q);
    while (q--) {
        int t; scanf("%d", &t);
        if (t == 1) { long long x; scanf("%lld", &x); base = x; ++epoch; continue; }
        int i; scanf("%d", &i); --i;
        if (stamp[i] != epoch) { val[i] = base; stamp[i] = epoch; }   // refresh
        if (t == 2) { long long x; scanf("%lld", &x); val[i] += x; }
        else printf("%lld\n", val[i]);
    }
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Eager:** $O(N)$ per assignment, $O(NQ)$ worst case in total; $O(N)$ space. **Reset only the touched cells:** $O(N + Q)$ in total (each touched entry is reset once), but a single assignment can still cost $O(Q)$. **Timestamps:** $O(1)$ worst case per query, $O(N + Q)$ in total; $O(N)$ space for the stamps.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **Overflow**: values reach $10^9 + 2\cdot10^5 \cdot 10^9$, far beyond 32 bits; use 64-bit integers (`long long`).
- **The initial array** counts as written at epoch $0$, so `stamp` starts at $0$ and no refresh happens before the first assignment.
- **Several assignments in a row**: only the last `base` matters, and the clock comparison `stamp[i] != epoch` does not care how many epochs a cell missed.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Refreshing after the add** instead of before: the add would be applied to a stale value and then overwritten by `base`.
- **Comparing `stamp[i] < epoch` with a clock that can wrap**: with a 32-bit clock and at most $2\cdot10^5$ assignments this cannot happen here, but in long-running systems it can; `!=` with a wide counter is the safe test.
:::

**Variants.** The same refresh-on-touch pattern implements "reset all to zero" in $O(1)$ for arrays reused across test cases (@sec-arr-multitest), and per-row versions of it give "assign a whole row" queries on a matrix (@sec-mat).

::: {.practice}
- [LC 1622 · Fancy Sequence](https://leetcode.com/problems/fancy-sequence/){difficulty="Hard"} — "add to all" and "multiply all" queries: keep one global affine map and store each element relative to the map in force when it was appended, the timestamp idea with a transform instead of a value.
:::
